Privacy search engine company DuckDuckGo has released a new survey revealing how much personal information users are sharing with AI chatbots, and how little many of them understand about where those conversations go. Here's what you need to know.

Survey shows AI users share more data than they realise

DuckDuckGo highlighted several privacy concerns related to people's use of AI chatbots in a survey released today, including the fact that nearly a third of users have told an AI something they wouldn't tell a friend, family member, co-worker, or even a medical professional. Among self-described AI enthusiasts, that figure rises to 56%.

Here is what DuckDuckGo had to say:

The company noted that, out of roughly 2,000 American adults surveyed, 53% did not know or were unsure that most chatbots use conversations by default to train on, while only 25% knew that AI chat logs can be obtained by law enforcement through a court subpoena.

The findings also showed a clear behavioural difference between those with and without children, with parents or guardians in households with kids almost twice as likely to confide in AI as those without. "Among parents using AI, 43% have told an AI something they have never shared with anyone," DuckDuckGo said, adding that "for AI users without children in the household, that figure drops to 25%."

DuckDuckGo argues that AI companies have been encouraging this behaviour, promoting chatbots as confidants in advertising and media appearances, despite the fact that these conversations may not be as private as users believe.

On the question of trust, the survey found that people have slightly more confidence in large AI companies than in the US government to protect their data. Both, however, are viewed with significant suspicion: 39% said they have no trust at all in major AI companies, compared to 48% who said the same about the government.

Finally, DuckDuckGo argues that users still have an opportunity to change how they approach AI privacy, particularly because chatbot usage habits are still emerging:

"When we talk about online privacy with search engines and browsers, a lot of people think, 'It's too late, my data is already out there.' But the most valuable data you can share with a tech giant is the next question you ask, not the ones you asked days, months, or even years ago. So it's never too late to switch to more private online services," the company said.

The company also reminded users that they can take proactive steps to protect their privacy when using AI chatbots, including choosing services with clearer, more transparent data-handling policies.
